pos: n. (the weighted rod on which thread is twisted; the emblem of the virtuous woman's industry)
etymology: Old English spinel, from spinnan, to spin. It renders Hebrew pelek, a whorl or round weight — the same word used of the district or circuit a man rules, since both are round.
biblical_def: She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her hands hold the distaff. Two tools and four mentions of hands in a single verse. The distaff held the mass of unspun wool or flax; the spindle was the weighted rod that twisted it into thread. Together they are the slowest technology in the ancient house — thread made one turn at a time, by a woman standing, for hours, to produce the raw material of everything her household would wear. Proverbs 31 puts this in the middle of a portrait that also includes buying a field, planting a vineyard, trading with merchant ships, and speaking with the law of kindness in her tongue. The spindle is not there to make her small. It is there because the chapter refuses to separate the visible from the invisible work: the same hands that hold the spindle are the hands she stretcheth out to the poor, and the same woman whose lamp goeth not out by night is praised by her husband in the gate. The chapter ends by asking that she be given of the fruit of her hands and that her own works praise her. Scripture's answer to hidden labour is not to call it unimportant but to call for it to be paid and publicly honoured.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the pin by which thread is formed, and on which it is wound; a slender rod turning on an axis.
webster_full: SPINDLE, n. The pin by which thread is formed, and on which it is wound.
SPINDLE, n. A slender pin or rod on which anything turns; an axis.
DISTAFF, n. The staff of a spinning wheel, to which a bunch of flax or tow is tied, and from which the thread is drawn.
SPIN, v.t. To draw out and twist into threads, either by the hand or machinery.
FLAX, n. A plant of the genus Linum, of whose fibrous skin thread is made.
scriptures: Proverbs 31:19
She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her hands hold the distaff.
Proverbs 31:13
She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands.
Proverbs 31:20
She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy.
Proverbs 31:31
Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 31 is used either to shrink a woman to a spindle or to be embarrassed by the spindle altogether; the chapter itself honours the hidden work and asks that it be publicly rewarded.
corruption_paragraphs: Two readings do damage to this chapter, and they are usually held by people arguing with each other. The first treats it as a checklist against which a wife is measured and found wanting — a portrait used as a rod. That is not how it is written. It is the instruction of a mother to a king about what sort of woman to look for, cast as an acrostic poem, and it ends in praise rather than in demand. Its subject buys, plants, trades, teaches, gives, and is honoured for all of it; nobody could do every item in one season, and the chapter never asks anyone to.

The second reading finds the spindle quaint and hurries to the vineyard and the merchant ships, as though household labour needed rescuing by commerce to be worth mentioning. Proverbs will not sort the work into tiers. It puts the spindle in the same list as the field and the ships and gives all of it the same verdict: let her own works praise her in the gates. Paul writes in the same spirit when he tells the younger women to be keepers at home and tells the whole church that whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men. The Lord who notices a cup of cold water has never once failed to notice thread.
roots_summary: Hebrew pelek (H6418), a whorl or spindle; kishor (H3601), the distaff; tsemer (H6785), wool; pishteh (H6593), flax or linen.
roots_lines: Hebrew pelek (H6418) — a round weight or whorl; the same word names a district, because both are circuits.
Hebrew kishor (H3601), the distaff — used only here in all of Scripture.
Hebrew tsemer (H6785) — wool; sought out by the woman before any thread is made.
Hebrew pishteh (H6593) — flax; the other raw material, and the stuff of priestly linen.
Hebrew kaph (H3709) — the palm; Proverbs 31 names her hands again and again, four times in two verses.
usage: “She layeth her hands to the spindle” — the slowest work in the house.
“She stretcheth out her hand to the poor” — the same hands, the next verse.
“let her own works praise her in the gates” — hidden labour publicly honoured.

pos: n. (the instrument thrown across a loom to carry the weft; Job's figure for the speed of life)
etymology: Old English scytel, a dart or missile, from sceotan, to shoot — the shuttle is named for how fast it is thrown. It renders Hebrew ereg, from a root meaning to weave.
biblical_def: My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope. Job is not writing poetry for its own sake; he is on an ash heap, and the figure is chosen for exactness. A weaver throws the shuttle across the warp and it is already at the other side — the fastest motion in a room otherwise full of slow work. And the weaving is going somewhere: every pass adds a line to a cloth Job cannot see, on a loom he is not operating. He returns to it repeatedly. Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good. Man cometh forth like a flower and is cut down, he fleeth also as a shadow and continueth not. David says the same without the suffering: thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee. Scripture's treatment of the brevity of life never ends in resignation. Moses draws the conclusion — so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. And Job, who said his days were spent without hope, is the same man who said I know that my redeemer liveth. The shuttle is fast. The weaver is faithful.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an instrument used by weavers for shooting the thread of the woof in weaving, from one side of the web to the other.
webster_full: SHUTTLE, n. An instrument used by weavers for shooting the thread of the woof in weaving from one side of the web to the other.
WEAVE, v.t. To unite threads of any kind in such a manner as to form cloth.
WARP, n. The threads which are extended lengthwise in the loom, and crossed by the woof.
WOOF, n. The threads that cross the warp in weaving; the weft.
HANDBREADTH, n. A space equal to the breadth of the hand; a palm.
scriptures: Job 7:6
My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope.
Job 9:25
Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good.
Job 14:2
He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not.
Psalm 39:5
Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth; and mine age is as nothing before thee: verily every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Selah.
corruption_summary: The brevity of life is answered either by denial — a culture that hides its dying — or by the counsel to seize the day for oneself; Scripture uses the shuttle to drive a man toward wisdom and a Redeemer.
corruption_paragraphs: Our age has arranged not to see the loom. Death happens elsewhere, age is a problem to be corrected, and the word mortality has been replaced by talk of wellness and longevity. The effect is not that men fear death less but that they meet it unprepared and alone. Scripture takes the opposite approach: it makes a man look. My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle. Mine age is as nothing before thee. It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment. The looking is not morbid; it is the only honest ground on which a life can be planned.

The alternative counsel — seize the day, since it is short — Scripture also knows and quotes: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die. Paul cites it as the logical position of a man with no resurrection, which is precisely what makes it useless for anyone who has one. The biblical conclusion from a fast shuttle is never spend it on yourself. It is so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom; it is to redeem the time, because the days are evil; it is Job, whose days were spent without hope, still saying that though worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God.
roots_summary: Hebrew ereg (H708), a weaver's shuttle or loom; arag (H707), to weave; hevel (H1892), vapour or vanity; tophach (H2947), a handbreadth.
roots_lines: Hebrew ereg (H708) — the weaver's shuttle; the swiftest thing in a room of slow work.
Hebrew arag (H707) — to weave; the trade behind the figure, and the work of Bezaleel's craftsmen.
Hebrew hevel (H1892) — a breath, a vapour; Ecclesiastes' verdict on the same brevity.
Hebrew tsel (H6738) — a shadow; he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not.
Greek atmis (G822) — a vapour; James asks what your life is, and answers with it.
usage: “swifter than a weaver's shuttle” — the fastest motion Job could name.
“they flee away, they see no good” — the figure pressed again.
“mine age is as nothing before thee” — measured against the one who is not brief.

pos: n. (a seat without a back; in Exodus, the birthing stool of the Hebrew midwives)
etymology: Old English stol, a seat or throne — the word once covered any seat, and narrowed later to a backless one. In 2 Kings it renders Hebrew kisse, a seat; in Exodus, obnayim, a pair of stones, the birthing stool.
biblical_def: The word carries two very different scenes. The first is quiet hospitality. The Shunammite woman perceives that Elisha is a holy man of God passing by continually, and says to her husband, Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick. Four items, named one by one: somewhere to sleep, somewhere to eat, somewhere to sit, and light. That is the whole architecture of hospitality, and it cost a woman who had no son a good deal of thought about a man who could not repay her. The second scene is the opposite of a welcome. Pharaoh instructs the Hebrew midwives: when ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them upon the stools; if it be a son, then ye shall kill him. The stools here are the birthing stones, the place where a woman labours, turned by a king's decree into an execution site. But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive. Two stools: one set out for a prophet by a woman who feared God, one used against infants by a king who did not, and defied by two women who did.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a seat without a back; a little form consisting of a board with three or four legs, intended as a seat for one person.
webster_full: STOOL, n. A seat without a back; a little form consisting of a board with three or four legs.
STOOL, n. The seat used in certain offices and conditions of life.
MIDWIFE, n. A woman that assists other women in childbirth.
CHAMBER, n. An apartment in an upper story, or in the story above the lower floor of a dwelling house.
HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward.
scriptures: 2 Kings 4:10

Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick: and it shall be, when he cometh to us, that he shall turn in thither.
Exodus 1:16
And he said, When ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them upon the stools; if it be a son, then ye shall kill him: but if it be a daughter, then she shall live.
Exodus 1:17
But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive.
Hebrews 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
corruption_summary: Hospitality has become entertaining — a performance for people who can reciprocate — and the midwives' defiance is claimed by every side of the abortion argument; Scripture names the stool in both scenes and says who feared God.
corruption_paragraphs: The Shunammite's four items rebuke the modern practice of hospitality almost by accident. She did not clean a house for guests who would return the favour; she built a room on the wall for a travelling preacher, furnished it plainly, and asked nothing. Christ states the principle: when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind; and thou shalt be blessed, for they cannot recompense thee. Where hospitality becomes entertaining, the guest list changes, the standard rises, and the poor stop being invited. A bed, a table, a stool and a candle are enough, and always were.

Exodus 1 is quoted constantly in the argument over the killing of infants, and it deserves to be, but the verse has more in it than a slogan. The midwives are named — Shiphrah and Puah, two working women whose names outlasted the Pharaoh's — and the text gives their reason: they feared God. They disobeyed the highest authority in the world, at risk of their lives, over the lives of children who were not theirs, and God dealt well with them and made them houses. That is the pattern for civil disobedience in Scripture: not conscience as preference, but the fear of God overriding a command to shed innocent blood, accepted with the consequences.
roots_summary: Hebrew kisse (H3678), a seat or throne; obnayim (H70), the birthing stones; yare (H3372), to fear; meyalledet, the midwife.
roots_lines: Hebrew kisse (H3678) — a seat, and also a throne; the plain stool in Elisha's chamber shares a word with Solomon's throne.
Hebrew obnayim (H70) — a pair of stones; the birthing stool, and elsewhere the potter's wheel.
Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear, to reverence; the stated reason the midwives disobeyed.
Hebrew ner (H5216) — a lamp; the fourth item the Shunammite set in the chamber.
Greek philoxenia (G5381) — love of strangers; the New Testament word rendered hospitality.
usage: “a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick” — the whole architecture of hospitality.
“see them upon the stools” — a birthing place turned into a decree.
“But the midwives feared God” — the reason given for the refusal.

pos: n. (a flat clay brick used for building or for drawing upon; Ezekiel's map of a besieged city)
etymology: Old English tigele, from Latin tegula, from tegere, to cover. In Ezekiel it renders Hebrew lebenah, a brick — the same word used of the bricks Israel made in Egypt.
biblical_def: Thou also, son of man, take thee a tile, and lay it before thee, and pourtray upon it the city, even Jerusalem. Ezekiel is told to draw a map on a clay brick — the ordinary building material of Babylon, where he was in exile — and then to besiege it: lay siege against it, build a fort, cast a mount, set the camp, set battering rams round about. A grown prophet playing with a brick in the street, in front of people who had lost that city, acting out what was about to happen to what was left of it. Ezekiel's ministry is full of these enacted signs because words had stopped landing. The other tiles in Scripture are a roof. When four men could not get their paralysed friend to Jesus through the crowd, they went upon the housetop, and let him down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus; Mark says plainly that they uncovered the roof and broke it up. They wrecked somebody's house to get a man to Christ, and the Lord, seeing their faith, forgave his sins and healed him without a word about the roof. One tile bears a siege, the other bears a hole; both were clay in the hands of men who believed God meant what he said.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a plate or piece of baked clay used for covering the roofs of buildings; a thin plate of baked clay.
webster_full: TILE, n. A plate or piece of baked clay used for covering the roofs of buildings.
TILING, n. A roof covered with tiles; tiles in general.
BRICK, n. A mass of earth, chiefly clay, first moistened and made fine by working, then formed into a long square and baked.
PORTRAY, v.t. To paint or draw the likeness of anything in colors; to describe in words.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
scriptures: Ezekiel 4:1
Thou also, son of man, take thee a tile, and lay it before thee, and pourtray upon it the city, even Jerusalem:
Ezekiel 4:2
And lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about.
Luke 5:19
And when they could not find by what way they might bring him in because of the multitude, they went upon the housetop, and let him down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus.
Mark 2:4
And when they could not come nigh unto him for the press, they uncovered the roof where he was: and when they had broken it up, they let down the bed wherein the sick of the palsy lay.
corruption_summary: Dramatized preaching is mistaken for Ezekiel's sign-acts, and persistence in bringing people to Christ is mistaken for pressure; both scenes were obedience under cost, ordered or rewarded by God himself.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Ezekiel's brick was commanded, not invented. He did not devise a memorable illustration to hold an audience; God told him to take the tile, and then told him to lie on his side for three hundred and ninety days, and to eat bread baked in a measured way. The sign-acts are prophecy in another medium, given by the Lord to a prophet whose people would not hear words. A preacher who stages a spectacle of his own choosing is doing the opposite of what Ezekiel did, however similar it looks from the back of the room.

The four men who broke up a roof teach the other half. They had one aim, they met a real obstacle, and they went through the obstacle rather than home. Mark notes what Jesus saw: when Jesus saw their faith — theirs, the carriers', not only the sick man's. There is such a thing as pressing a person toward Christ in a way that is merely pressure, and Scripture has no interest in that. But there is also a quiet unbelief that calls its own passivity respect. These men dug through clay tiles over somebody else's head, and the Lord commended them for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew lebenah (H3843), a brick or tile; matsor (H4692), a siege; Greek keramos (G2766), a roof tile; apostegazo (G648), to unroof.
roots_lines: Hebrew lebenah (H3843) — a brick; the same word as the bricks of Egyptian bondage, now a map of Jerusalem.
Hebrew matsor (H4692) — siege, entrenchment; what Ezekiel was told to build against his own clay city.
Greek keramos (G2766) — a roof tile, potter's clay; the tiling Luke says they let him through.
Greek apostegazo (G648) — to unroof, to take off the covering; Mark's blunt verb for what they did.
Hebrew oth (H226) — a sign; Ezekiel is told the whole performance is a sign to the house of Israel.
usage: “take thee a tile... and pourtray upon it the city” — prophecy drawn on a brick.
“let him down through the tiling” — a roof opened to reach Christ.
“when they had broken it up” — Mark's account of the cost.

pos: n. pl. (leather straps used to bind a prisoner for scourging)
etymology: Old English thwang, a narrow strip of leather. In Acts it renders Greek himas, a leather strap — the same word John the Baptist uses of the latchet of a shoe he was not worthy to unloose.
biblical_def: Paul has been dragged out of the temple and nearly killed by a mob, and the Roman chief captain, unable to make out the cause from the shouting, orders the standard procedure: bade that he should be examined by scourging. Examination by scourging meant beating a man until he said something useful. They were stretching him out and binding him with thongs when Paul asked a single question of the centurion standing by: Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned? The effect was immediate. Those who should have examined him departed; the chief captain was afraid, because he had bound him. Paul had used the same right at Philippi, and pointedly — they have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily. Two things stand together here without contradiction. Paul suffered enormously and never demanded exemption from suffering for Christ; and Paul used every lawful protection a citizen had, and used it in a way that publicly embarrassed officials who had broken their own law. The thongs teach that a Christian may appeal to Caesar's statute without ceasing to belong to Christ's kingdom.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a strap of leather, used for fastening anything; a narrow strip of hide.
webster_full: THONG, n. A strap of leather, used for fastening anything.
SCOURGE, n. A whip; a lash consisting of a strap or cord.
SCOURGE, v.t. To whip severely; to lash; to punish with severity.
CITIZEN, n. A native or permanent inhabitant of a city, or one who has the freedom and privileges of the city in which he resides.
UNCONDEMNED, a. Not condemned; not tried and found guilty.
scriptures: Acts 22:25
And as they bound him with thongs, Paul said unto the centurion that stood by, Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?
Acts 22:24
The chief captain commanded him to be brought into the castle, and bade that he should be examined by scourging; that he might know wherefore they cried so against him.
Acts 22:29
Then straightway they departed from him which should have examined him: and the chief captain also was afraid, after he knew that he was a Roman, and because he had bound him.
Acts 16:37

But Paul said unto them, They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast us into prison; and now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us out.
corruption_summary: Christians are told either that claiming a legal right is unspiritual or that grievance is itself a witness; Paul used his citizenship sparingly, lawfully, and for the sake of the gospel's progress rather than his own comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: One kind of piety holds that a believer should simply absorb every injustice, and treats Paul's appeal to Rome as a lapse. The record does not support it. The same Paul who was five times beaten with forty stripes save one, thrice beaten with rods, once stoned, and who wrote of being pressed out of measure, also stood on his citizenship at Philippi and at Jerusalem and finally said I appeal unto Caesar. He did not seek out suffering, and he did not flee it. He used the law where the law protected the work, and he bore what the law would not prevent. Christ himself, struck before the high priest, asked why smitest thou me.

The reverse error is now more common: a Christianity trained to look for offence, quick with a complaint, treating its own grievances as evidence of faithfulness. Paul's appeals are strikingly few for a man so often mistreated, and each one serves the mission rather than his comfort — at Philippi so the new church would not be left under a cloud of illegality, at Jerusalem so he could keep preaching, at Caesarea so he could testify in Rome. Peter draws the line for everyone else: let none of you suffer as a busybody in other men's matters; yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed.
roots_summary: Greek himas (G2438), a leather strap or thong; mastizo (G3147), to scourge; akatakritos (G178), uncondemned; Rhomaios (G4514), a Roman.
roots_lines: Greek himas (G2438) — a leather strap; used of these thongs and of the shoe latchet John was unworthy to unloose.
Greek mastizo (G3147) — to scourge with the flagellum, a punishment Roman citizens were exempt from.
Greek akatakritos (G178) — uncondemned, untried; the exact word of Paul's objection in both cities.
Greek politeia (G4174) — citizenship; the chief captain bought his with a great sum, Paul was free born.
Greek epikaleomai (G1941) — to appeal; I appeal unto Caesar, the final use of the same right.
usage: “as they bound him with thongs” — the preparation interrupted by a question.
“examined by scourging” — the standard procedure Paul stopped.
“the chief captain also was afraid” — the law turned back on the lawless.

pos: n. (a bandage rolled around a broken limb to splint it; in Ezekiel, the splint God withholds)
etymology: From roll, Old French roller, from Latin rotula, a little wheel. In Ezekiel it renders Hebrew chittul, a bandage or swathe, from a root meaning to wrap.
biblical_def: Ezekiel is given one of the most specific judgments in Scripture, and it turns on a medical detail. Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and, lo, it shall not be bound up to be healed, to put a roller to bind it, to make it strong to hold the sword. A roller is a splint bandage. Set and wrapped, a broken arm knits and holds a sword again; left unbound, it heals crooked or not at all. God says he broke the arm and will not permit the splint. Then he goes further: I will break his arms, the strong, and that which was broken — both arms, the sound one and the injured one, so that the sword falls out of his hand. The withheld bandage is the whole judgment, because it is not the breaking that finishes a nation but the refusal of healing. Set against this is what God does for his own. Isaiah describes Judah's wounds and bruises and putrifying sores as not closed, neither bound up, neither mollified with ointment — and the book that says so is the book that says he was wounded for our transgressions and with his stripes we are healed. And the Samaritan on the Jericho road bound up the wounds of a man who was nothing to him, pouring in oil and wine. A roller in the hand is mercy; a roller withheld is judgment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): that which rolls; a bandage; a fillet; a long and broad bandage used in surgery.
webster_full: ROLLER, n. That which rolls; that which turns on its own axis.
ROLLER, n. A bandage; a fillet; a long and broad bandage used in surgery.
BANDAGE, n. A fillet, roller, or swath, used in dressing and binding up wounds.
SPLINT, n. A piece of wood or other substance used by surgeons to hold a fractured bone in its place.
MOLLIFY, v.t. To soften; to make tender; to assuage, as pain or irritation.
scriptures: Ezekiel 30:21
Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and, lo, it shall not be bound up to be healed, to put a roller to bind it, to make it strong to hold the sword.
Ezekiel 30:22
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and will break his arms, the strong, and that which was broken; and I will cause the sword to fall out of his hand.
Isaiah 1:6
From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores: they have not been closed, neither bound up, neither mollified with ointment.
Luke 10:34
And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
corruption_summary: Judgment is thought incompatible with a God of love, so passages like Ezekiel 30 are quietly dropped; the withheld roller shows judgment as God's deliberate act toward the proud, in the same Bible where he binds up the brokenhearted.
corruption_paragraphs: A God who breaks an arm and forbids the splint is not the God of the popular imagination, and the usual solution is to treat such passages as the primitive layer of an evolving book. Scripture does not permit the surgery. The prophet who writes Ezekiel 30 writes Ezekiel 34, where God says I will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick. The same hand, the same book, the same chapter-length care about bandages. What changes is not God's character but the person before him: Pharaoh, who had called the river his own and made it, and the scattered sheep of a shepherdless flock.

There is a matching error inside the church, which is to hold the doctrine of judgment and lose the trade of binding up. Isaiah's complaint against Judah is not that its wounds were undeserved but that nobody had closed them — not bound up, neither mollified with ointment. The Samaritan, who owed the man nothing and whose people were despised by him, poured in oil and wine and paid for the room. Christ told that story to a lawyer who wanted the definition of neighbour narrowed, and ended it with two words that leave no room for theory: Go, and do thou likewise.
roots_summary: Hebrew chittul (H2848), a bandage or swathe; chabash (H2280), to bind up; zeroa (H2220), the arm; Greek katadeo (G2611), to bind up a wound.
roots_lines: Hebrew chittul (H2848) — a splint bandage; used only here, in the judgment on Pharaoh.
Hebrew chabash (H2280) — to bind up, to bandage; what God does for the brokenhearted and refuses to Egypt.
Hebrew zeroa (H2220) — the arm; the standing figure for a nation's military strength.
Greek katadeo (G2611) — to bind up; used once, of the Samaritan on the Jericho road.
Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal; the healing the splint would have permitted.
usage: “it shall not be bound up to be healed” — the judgment is the withheld bandage.
“neither bound up, neither mollified with ointment” — a nation nobody tended.
“bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine” — the roller in a stranger's hand.

pos: n. (the line where two pieces of cloth are joined; the coat of Christ had none)
etymology: Old English seam, a joining, from the root of sew. In John it appears in the compound Greek araphos — a-, without, and a root meaning to sew together: seamless, unsewn.
biblical_def: John records what the soldiers did with the clothes of a dying man, and records it because it fulfilled a psalm written a thousand years earlier. They made four parts of his garments, one to every soldier, and also his coat: now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout. A seamless garment could not be quartered without being destroyed, so they said, let us not rend it, but cast lots for it. Psalm 22 had said both things in one verse — they part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture — two distinct actions that look like Hebrew parallelism until four Roman soldiers accidentally perform them separately at the foot of a cross. John names the coincidence for what it is: that the scripture might be fulfilled. The seamlessness has drawn comment since the earliest centuries, some noting that the high priest's robe was likewise woven whole. Scripture itself does not press the figure, and neither should we press it further than the text. What the text does say is that the last garment of Christ was one piece that men would not tear, at the very hour they were tearing him, and that Paul afterward asks a divided church to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the suture or joining of two edges of cloth by the needle; a line of junction; a cicatrix or scar.
webster_full: SEAM, n. The suture or joining of two edges of cloth by the needle.
SEAM, n. A line of junction; the joint or juncture of planks in a ship's side or deck.
SEAMLESS, a. Having no seam; as the seamless garment of Christ.
VESTURE, n. Garment; habit; external covering.
LOT, n. That which, in human speech, is called chance, hazard, fortune; but in strictness of language, is the determination of Providence.
scriptures: John 19:23
Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments, and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also his coat: now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.
John 19:24

They said therefore among themselves, Let us not rend it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be: that the scripture might be fulfilled, which saith, They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots. These things therefore the soldiers did.
Psalm 22:18
They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture.
Ephesians 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
corruption_summary: The seamless coat is pressed into an argument for institutional union at any cost; John reports it as a fulfilled prophecy, and Paul's unity is of the Spirit, kept rather than manufactured, and bounded by one faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The seamless robe has been used for centuries as an emblem of a single visible church, and any separation cast as tearing the coat of Christ. It is a powerful image and it proves nothing, because John does not use it that way; he uses it to show a psalm fulfilled to the letter by men who had never read it. Where Scripture does address unity it is careful: Paul asks the Ephesians to keep the unity of the Spirit, not to build it — it already exists and is the Spirit's — and he grounds it on one Lord, one faith, one baptism. A union assembled by men over the top of contradictory faiths is not that unity and cannot be kept, because it was never given.

The other abuse is to make the passage a licence for easy division, as though doctrinal precision excused a quarrelsome spirit. Paul's endeavouring is a strong word; the same letter asks for all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love. Christ prayed that they all may be one, that the world may believe. A church that separates without grief, or over matters the Scripture nowhere makes terms of communion, has not honoured the prayer offered hours before the soldiers looked at that coat and decided it was too good to tear.
roots_summary: Greek araphos (G729), without seam; chiton (G5509), the inner coat; himation (G2440), the outer garment; klhros (G2819), a lot.
roots_lines: Greek araphos (G729) — unsewn, seamless; used once in Scripture, of the coat of Christ.
Greek chiton (G5509) — the tunic worn next to the body; the seamless piece.
Greek himation (G2440) — the outer garments; the four parts the soldiers divided.
Greek kleros (G2819) — a lot; cast for the coat, and the root behind clergy and inheritance.
Hebrew levush (H3830) — clothing, vesture; the word of Psalm 22:18.
usage: “the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout” — a garment that could not be quartered.
“Let us not rend it, but cast lots for it” — prophecy fulfilled by men who did not know it.
“the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” — unity kept, not constructed.

pos: v.t. (to cut into small pieces; used of the wild gourds cast into the prophets' pot)
etymology: Old English screade, a piece cut off — related to shroud and to German Schrot. In 2 Kings it renders Hebrew palach, to cleave or slice open.
biblical_def: There was a dearth in the land, and the sons of the prophets were sitting before Elisha at Gilgal, and he told his servant to set on the great pot and seethe pottage for them. One of them went out to gather herbs, and found a wild vine, and gathered thereof wild gourds his lap full, and came and shred them into the pot of pottage: for they knew them not. The last clause is the whole trouble. He was not lazy, he was not malicious, and he was not idle — he went out in a famine and came back with a lapful. He simply did not know what he had picked, and he shredded it into the common pot before anyone could look at it. They poured out for the men to eat, and they cried out, O thou man of God, there is death in the pot. Elisha called for meal, cast it in, and said pour out for the people; and there was no harm in the pot. The story is small and it is not about cooking. Poison entered the company of the prophets through a sincere man doing a generous thing with something he had not identified, and the remedy came from the man of God. Paul's instruction stands in the same line: prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to cut into small pieces, particularly narrow and long pieces, as of cloth or leather; a small piece cut off.
webster_full: SHRED, v.t. To cut into small pieces, particularly narrow and long pieces, as of cloth or leather.
SHRED, n. A long narrow piece cut off; a strip; a fragment.
POTTAGE, n. A species of food composed of meat and vegetables boiled to softness in water.
DEARTH, n. Scarcity which renders dear; want; need; famine.
GOURD, n. A plant of the genus Cucurbita, and its fruit.
scriptures: 2 Kings 4:39
And one went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine, and gathered thereof wild gourds his lap full, and came and shred them into the pot of pottage: for they knew them not.
2 Kings 4:38

And Elisha came again to Gilgal: and there was a dearth in the land; and the sons of the prophets were sitting before him: and he said unto his servant, Set on the great pot, and seethe pottage for the sons of the prophets.
2 Kings 4:40

So they poured out for the men to eat. And it came to pass, as they were eating of the pottage, that they cried out, and said, O thou man of God, there is death in the pot. And they could not eat thereof.
2 Kings 4:41
But he said, Then bring meal. And he cast it into the pot; and he said, Pour out for the people, that they may eat. And there was no harm in the pot.
corruption_summary: Sincerity is treated as its own safeguard — a teaching is judged by the earnestness of the man bringing it; the sons of the prophets ate death from a pot filled by a sincere man who had not identified what he gathered.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing rule of the age is that sincerity sanctifies. If a man means well, his contribution is welcome; to examine it is thought unkind. This little narrative was written for that error. The gatherer meant nothing but good — there was a famine, he went to the field, he filled his lap, he came back and put it straight into the common pot. Nothing was wrong with his motive and everything was wrong with his gourds, and the note the Spirit adds is for they knew them not. The company of the prophets nearly died of an honest mistake, which is why John says try the spirits, and the Bereans are commended for searching the scriptures daily whether those things were so.

The story also quietly rebukes the opposite temper. When death was found in the pot, nobody was named, shamed, or expelled; Elisha called for meal. The remedy was applied by the man of God, the meal was cast in, and the people ate. There is a way of guarding a church that poisons it in another manner — suspicion in every direction, the pot never poured because something might be in it. Prove all things, Paul says, and then: hold fast that which is good. Both halves. The pot was meant to be eaten from.
roots_summary: Hebrew palach (H6398), to cleave or slice; nazid (H5138), pottage; qemach (H7058), meal or flour; raab (H7458), famine or dearth.
roots_lines: Hebrew palach (H6398) — to cleave, to slice open; rendered shred here.
Hebrew nazid (H5138) — boiled pottage; the same word as the mess Jacob sold to Esau.
Hebrew qemach (H7058) — meal; cast into the pot at Elisha's word, as salt was cast into the spring at Jericho.
Hebrew raab (H7458) — famine, dearth; the pressure under which the mistake was made.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove; prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
usage: “shred them into the pot of pottage: for they knew them not” — sincerity without identification.
“there is death in the pot” — discovered at the table, not in the field.
“Then bring meal” — the remedy from the man of God, and the pot still poured.

pos: n. (a long strip of cloth wound about a newborn; in Job, what God wraps the sea in)
etymology: From swaddle, a frequentative of Old English swathian, to bind or wrap, plus band. In Job it renders Hebrew chathullah, a swathing band; in Luke, Greek sparganoo, to wrap in strips of cloth.
biblical_def: God answers Job out of the whirlwind by asking who shut up the sea with doors when it brake forth as if it had issued out of the womb — when I made the cloud the garment thereof, and thick darkness a swaddlingband for it. The ocean is a newborn, and God wrapped it. That is the scale of the figure: the thing men find most uncontrollable was swaddled at birth by the one now speaking, who set bars and doors and said hitherto shalt thou come, but no further. Then the same word turns up in a stable. She brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger. The one who swaddled the sea consented to be swaddled. And the sign given to shepherds was not the glory that had just filled the sky but the cloth: ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. Ezekiel makes the third use and it is the dark one — Jerusalem as an infant whose navel was not cut, not washed, not salted, nor swaddled at all, cast out in the open field, until the LORD passed by and said unto her, Live. To be swaddled is to be claimed. The sea was, the Son was, and the abandoned child was.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a band or cloth wrapped round an infant; a swathe; that which is bound about a newborn child.
webster_full: SWADDLING-BAND, n. A band or cloth wrapped round an infant.
SWADDLE, v.t. To swathe; to bind, as a child, with cloths or bandages.
SWATHE, v.t. To bind with a band, bandage or rollers.
MANGER, n. A trough or box in which fodder is laid for cattle.
NATIVITY, n. Birth; the coming into life or the world.
scriptures: Job 38:9
When I made the cloud the garment thereof, and thick darkness a swaddlingband for it,
Luke 2:7
And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
Luke 2:12
And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger.
Ezekiel 16:4
And as for thy nativity, in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee; thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all.
corruption_summary: The nativity is sentimentalized until the swaddling clothes are decoration; Scripture makes them a sign given to working men, and puts the same word in the mouth of God describing how he wrapped the sea.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the details of the nativity are given as evidence and not as atmosphere. The angel does not tell the shepherds to look for a glow or a feeling; he gives them two verifiable particulars — swaddling clothes and a manger — so that when they came with haste they could know they had found the right child. Luke, who says he traced all things from the very first to write an orderly account, records the cloth because it was reported by men who saw it.

The second thing worth holding is the distance the word travels. In Job, God swaddles the sea in thick darkness, an image of absolute mastery over what no man can govern. In Luke, the same act is performed upon him by a young mother in a borrowed shelter. Paul states the doctrine without the picture: he made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant. Between the ocean wrapped at its birth and the infant wrapped in a stable there is one person, and the second fact is only astonishing if the first is believed.

roots_lines: Hebrew chathullah (H2854) — a swaddling band; used once, of the thick darkness around the newborn sea.
Hebrew chathal (H2853) — to swathe; nor swaddled at all in Ezekiel's account of abandoned Jerusalem.
Greek sparganoo (G4683) — to wrap in swaddling strips; used twice, both in Luke 2.
Greek phatne (G5336) — a manger or feeding trough; the other half of the sign given to the shepherds.
Greek prototokos (G4416) — firstborn; she brought forth her firstborn son.
usage: “thick darkness a swaddlingband for it” — the sea wrapped at its birth.
“wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger” — the wrapper wrapped.
“nor swaddled at all” — the child nobody claimed, until God did.

pos: n. (a cover; in 2 Kings, the bored cover of the chest that funded the temple repairs)
etymology: Old English hlid, a cover or door, from a root meaning to cover. In 2 Kings it renders Hebrew deleth, a door — the chest's cover is called its door, and a hole was bored through it.
biblical_def: Joash had ordered the house of the LORD repaired, and for twenty-three years nothing was done; the priests collected money from their acquaintance and the breaches went unmended. So the king changed the system, and the whole reform turns on a carpentry detail. Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in the lid of it, and set it beside the altar, on the right side as one cometh into the house of the LORD, and the priests that kept the door put in all the money that was brought. A sealed box with a hole in the top, standing in public, beside the altar, where everyone entering could see it. Money went in and did not come out until the king's scribe and the high priest came together, counted it, and put it in bags — two officials, never one. Then it went straight to masons and hewers of stone and timber, to repair the breaches of the house of the LORD. And the text adds the line every treasurer should want written about him: they reckoned not with the men, into whose hand they delivered the money to be bestowed on workmen: for they dealt faithfully. Centuries later Jesus sat over against the treasury and watched what people put in. The box is still being watched.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a cover; that which shuts the opening of a vessel or box; the cover of the eye.
webster_full: LID, n. A cover; that which shuts the opening of a vessel or box.
LID, n. The cover of the eye; the membrane which is drawn over the eyeball at pleasure.
CHEST, n. A box of wood or other material, in which goods are kept or transported.
TREASURY, n. A place or building in which stores of wealth are reposited; the place where the public revenues are deposited.
FAITHFUL, a. Firm in adherence to the truth and to the duties of religion; true to one's trust.
scriptures: 2 Kings 12:9

But Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in the lid of it, and set it beside the altar, on the right side as one cometh into the house of the LORD: and the priests that kept the door put therein all the money that was brought into the house of the LORD.
2 Kings 12:10

And it was so, when they saw that there was much money in the chest, that the king's scribe and the high priest came up, and they put up in bags, and told the money that was found in the house of the LORD.
2 Kings 12:15
Moreover they reckoned not with the men, into whose hand they delivered the money to be bestowed on workmen: for they dealt faithfully.
Mark 12:41
And Jesus sat over against the treasury, and beheld how the people cast money into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much.
corruption_summary: Financial accountability in a church is treated as worldly distrust or waved away by an appeal to integrity; Jehoiada built the safeguards into the furniture and the Spirit recorded the men's honesty as a separate fact.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite mistakes are made with church money, and 2 Kings 12 answers both. The first is to treat controls as unspiritual — we trust our pastor, we do not need two signatures — as though procedure insulted a brother. Jehoiada trusted his priests and still bored the hole, still set the chest in public beside the altar, still required the king's scribe and the high priest to open it together. Paul did the same, sending a brother chosen by the churches along with the collection, providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men. Controls do not accuse anyone; they protect everyone, the honest man most of all.

The second mistake is to build the system and stop caring about the men. Scripture refuses to let procedure replace character: they reckoned not with the men... for they dealt faithfully. The accounts were not audited because the workmen had proved trustworthy, which is a remarkable thing to record in a book so unsparing about Israel's kings. A congregation needs both — a chest with a hole in the lid, and men of whom that sentence could honestly be written. And over both stands the Lord who sat down opposite the treasury and watched, and whose verdict fell not on the amount but on what it cost the giver.
roots_summary: Hebrew deleth (H1817), a door or lid; aron (H727), a chest or ark; bedeq (H919), a breach needing repair; Greek gazophulakion (G1049), the treasury.
roots_lines: Hebrew deleth (H1817) — a door; the chest's cover is named as its door, and a hole was bored through it.
Hebrew aron (H727) — a chest; the same word as the ark of the covenant and as Joseph's coffin.
Hebrew bedeq (H919) — a breach or fissure; what the money was raised to repair.
Hebrew emunah (H530) — faithfulness; for they dealt faithfully.
Greek gazophulakion (G1049) — the temple treasury; where Christ sat and watched the giving.
usage: “bored a hole in the lid of it” — the reform built into the furniture.
“the king's scribe and the high priest came up” — never one man alone.
“for they dealt faithfully” — the sentence a treasurer should want written of him.
